profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] CyrusOne was founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten, who had previously built companies acquired by IXC Communications. Wikipedia coverage of CyrusOne states the company opened what it described as the largest data center in Texas in Carrollton in 2012, the anchor of the Dallas Fort Worth cluster that this registry row is part of, alongside CyrusOne buildings in nearby Allen, Lewisville, and Collin County. CyrusOne also operates a substantial San Antonio campus and an Austin facility, both long-running Texas markets for the company, though no specific acquisition or opening story for San Antonio or Austin individually was located in available sourcing this session. The company was acquired by ABRY Partners in 2007, purchased by Cincinnati Bell for 525 million dollars in 2010, completed an IPO in 2013, and was taken private again in 2022 when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts and Global Infrastructure Partners acquired it for 15 billion dollars. No building specific address or individual MW figures were located in available sourcing this session.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's Allen campus publishes 77 MW of IT capacity, making it the second-largest facility by disclosed power in Texas and representing 24 percent of the state's published total across mapped sites.

The 77 MW spanning three facility codes and roughly 976,000 square feet can support between 1,925 and 7,700 racks depending on power density. AI training typically demands 40 kW per rack, while legacy colocation uses 10 kW per rack. CyrusOne has not published the actual rack density or breakdown of workload types at this campus, so the true utilization model remains opaque.

The certifications indicate the campus can host payment processing, regulated health data, federal government workloads, and enterprise systems requiring audited security controls. These credentials determine what customers can legally place there, not what is currently running. Green Globes environmental certification sits separately from compliance credentials and does not signal specialized power or cooling infrastructure for high-density compute.

The 77 MW figure itself requires context. Only 8 of Texas's 133 mapped facilities have published megawatt counts, meaning the ranking reflects operator disclosure choices rather than actual statewide capacity distribution. This facility's prominent position in the published data does not indicate whether Texas's largest deployments have chosen to disclose their power consumption.
